title: On Bonart's interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law
authors: J. -P. Bouchaud, I. Mastromatteo, B. Toth
abstract: The square-root impact law (SRIL), $I = Yσ\sqrt{Q/V}$, bundles two facts that a single mechanism must explain at once: a shape (impact proportional to square-root of traded volume $Q$) and an amplitude ($Y=O(1)$, independent of the participation rate $\varphi$). Bonart has recently proposed an elegant solution: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart. We reformulate and simplify his argument, and foreground the ingredient he himself regards as essential --- that the market whitens the stationary stream of each participant's metaorders, not any isolated one. The Lillo--Mike--Farmer model satisfies his premises, yet gives an isolated metaorder the super-square-root impact $\varphi^{(1-γ)/2}Q^{(1+γ)/2}$, $γ\in(0,1)$, because single metaorders (i.e. not part of a stream) are statistically invisible and thus priced mechanically. We then construct an explicit multi-agent propagator that realizes Bonart's whitening, and show it reproduces the clean SRIL precisely when the market can attribute trades to their issuer. But correct re-attribution of anonymous trades is a formidable task, which requires markets to behave as implausibly efficient signal processing machines. The stream hypothesis makes a sharp, falsifiable prediction --- isolated metaorders, well separated in time, should not obey the SRIL --- that does not seem agree with empirical data known to us. Independently, a volume-conservation argument singles out the square-root law and lays bare the step the diffusivity route must assume: diffusivity fixes the variance of impact --- an additive, stationary, age-blind quantity --- whereas the SRIL is a law for the mean impact, which marginally decays as $1/\sqrt{\text{age}}$ and therefore demands an origin of time.
summary: This paper analyzes the theoretical underpinnings of the Square-Root Impact Law (SRIL) in financial markets. It argues that the law's consistency requires a specific scaling exponent ($\delta=1/2$) derived from volume conservation, suggesting the law stems from equating mean impact to standard deviation. The work highlights the tension between theoretical assumptions (like stream whitening) and observed market behavior.
main_problem: The paper seeks to reconcile the empirical Square-Root Impact Law (SRIL) in financial markets with a consistent theoretical mechanism derived from market microstructure physics.
main_result: A volume-conservation argument strongly selects the exponent $\delta=1/2$ for the impact law, suggesting the SRIL arises from a mean-equals-standard-deviation identification rather than purely diffusive processes.
method: The authors use mathematical derivations based on variance budgets, conservation laws, and comparing theoretical models (like the Lillo–Mike–Farmer model) against the required scaling behavior.
model_or_system: The system is a financial market microstructure, modeling the price impact ($I$) of metaorders ($Q$) relative to total volume ($V$) and volatility ($\sigma$). The analysis involves decomposing returns into background and impact components.
key_observables: Price impact ($I$), traded volume ($Q$), daily volatility ($\sigma$), and the participation rate ($\varphi$).
important_parameters: The exponent $\delta$ governing the power-law dependence of impact on volume, and the participation rate $\varphi$.
main_assumptions: The core assumptions involve the market whitening the *stream* of metaorders, and the analysis relies on volume-conservation arguments to constrain the scaling exponent $\delta$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the empirical requirements of the SRIL, then reviewing and simplifying Bonart's whitening argument, and finally using volume-conservation and scaling analysis to derive the necessary exponent $\delta=1/2$.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the rigorous mathematical techniques used—analyzing scaling laws, variance budgets, and the failure of simple diffusive assumptions—are highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems.
